vulnerabilities.name: Missing X-Frame-Options and CSP frame-ancestors
vulnerabilities.description: The response carries neither an X-Frame-Options header nor a Content-Security-Policy with a frame-ancestors directive, so the page can be embedded in an <iframe>/<frame>/<object> on any third-party origin.
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed by loading the target page inside a test iframe from an unrelated origin and observing it render rather than being blocked by the browser.

vulnerabilities.name: Weak X-Frame-Options Value (ALLOW-FROM / Unsupported Directive)
vulnerabilities.description: X-Frame-Options is set to ALLOW-FROM, a deprecated directive that modern browsers (Chrome, Edge, Safari) ignore entirely, causing them to fall back to allowing framing from any origin as if the header were absent.
vulnerabilities.notes: Flag regardless of the whitelisted origin named in ALLOW-FROM, since the directive itself is non-functional in most current browsers; a CSP frame-ancestors directive should be present as the real control.

vulnerabilities.name: frame-ancestors Allows Wildcard or Overly Broad Origins
vulnerabilities.description: The CSP frame-ancestors directive is present but set to * or to a broad pattern (e.g. https://*.example.com when example.com hosts untrusted user content on subdomains), still permitting framing from an effectively unrestricted or attacker-reachable set of origins.
vulnerabilities.notes: Especially relevant when the wildcarded parent domain allows user-controlled subdomains (e.g. a PaaS with *.example-paas.com tenants).

vulnerabilities.name: Conflicting X-Frame-Options and CSP frame-ancestors
vulnerabilities.description: The response sends both X-Frame-Options and a CSP frame-ancestors directive with inconsistent policies (e.g. X-Frame-Options: DENY alongside frame-ancestors allowing an origin, or vice versa). Per spec, browsers that support frame-ancestors ignore X-Frame-Options, so the effective policy may be looser than the X-Frame-Options value suggests.
vulnerabilities.notes: Verify actual browser behavior rather than assuming the stricter of the two headers wins; CSP frame-ancestors takes precedence in browsers that implement it.

vulnerabilities.name: Sensitive State-Changing Page Is Framable
vulnerabilities.description: A specific page that triggers a sensitive, irreversible, or state-changing action with a single click/tap (delete account, change email, authorize an OAuth grant, transfer funds, change password) lacks framing protection, making it a realistic clickjacking target even if the site has a general policy elsewhere.
vulnerabilities.notes: Check framing protection per-endpoint, not only on the login page; a global policy on static pages does not guarantee coverage of dynamically rendered sensitive actions.

vulnerabilities.name: JavaScript Frame-Busting Script as Sole Defense
vulnerabilities.description: The page relies only on a client-side frame-busting script (checking top !== self and reloading/breaking out) instead of X-Frame-Options/CSP, which can be neutralized via the sandbox attribute on the containing iframe, the Suppress Script Exceptions technique (onbeforeunload abuse), or simply double-framing.
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed bypassable when the embedding iframe carries sandbox="allow-scripts" without allow-top-navigation, which silently prevents the frame-busting script's own top.location reassignment from executing.

vulnerabilities.name: Drag-and-Drop / Scroll-Jacking Surface
vulnerabilities.description: A framable page exposes a drag-and-drop interaction (file upload target, draggable UI element, sortable list) that can be re-targeted by overlaying a transparent decoy, tricking the user into dragging sensitive data (e.g. an autofilled credential, a copied token) into an attacker-controlled drop target.
vulnerabilities.notes: Treat as a sub-variant of standard clickjacking; the same frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options fix also closes this surface.

vulnerabilities.name: Likejacking / Cursorjacking via CSS Opacity Overlay Surface
vulnerabilities.description: A framable page contains a small, single-purpose action button (social share/like, one-click subscribe, consent toggle) that is a realistic target for pixel-precise opacity-overlay clickjacking, where the real control is made nearly transparent and positioned beneath a decoy UI the user is lured into clicking.

vulnerabilities.name: Double-Click / Delayed-Click Interaction Bypassing Single-Click Guards
vulnerabilities.description: The page implements a client-side click-validation defense (requiring pointer movement, a short delay, or disabling the button until a real mouse event fires) intended to defeat clickjacking, but the control is still embeddable, and the requirement can be satisfied by a two-stage decoy (double-click clickjacking) that lures a genuine second click after an initial decoy interaction.
vulnerabilities.notes: Client-side interaction heuristics are not a substitute for frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options; flag whenever the underlying page is still framable regardless of the click-guard logic present.

vulnerabilities.name: Framable Login/OAuth Consent Page Enabling Credential or Grant Theft
vulnerabilities.description: A login form or OAuth/SSO consent screen is embeddable in a third-party frame, allowing invisible-iframe overlay techniques to trick the user into submitting credentials or approving an authorization grant that they believe they are not interacting with at all.
vulnerabilities.notes: Highest-severity variant of this class since a successful decoy can harvest credentials or an OAuth grant rather than just a single UI action.
